title: Polar vortex, early November 2026: what is forecast and what would count
summary: As of 30 October 2026 forecasts show the stratospheric polar vortex weakening in early November, but most do not show its winds fully reversing, and the official outlooks for 4-12 November favor above-normal temperatures across most of the United States, not a freeze. A confirmed 'sudden stratospheric warming' needs the winds to reverse, and any effect at the surface would take weeks. The tests below were fixed on 30 October, before the outcome.

sections.heading: What is the polar vortex?
paragraphs: The stratospheric polar vortex is a ring of strong west-to-east winds around the Arctic, roughly 10 to 50 km up. It normally strengthens through autumn. Forecasters follow it with the zonal-mean wind at 10 hPa and 60 degrees North [c1].

sections.heading: What is forecast (as issued on 30 October 2026)
paragraphs: The analysed wind rose to about +23 m/s around 27 October and fell to roughly +15 to +17 m/s on 29-30 October (read from a chart, approximate) [f1]. Forecast ensemble members fall toward about 0 to +5 m/s around 10-13 November; a few members dip slightly below zero [f2]. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (29 October) favors above-normal temperatures for most of the contiguous United States on 4-12 November, with probabilities above 70 percent from the Mid-Atlantic to the Great Lakes for 4-8 November, and lists West Coast rain, snow and wind risks but no cold hazard [f3].

sections.heading: What would count as a sudden stratospheric warming
paragraphs: By the usual convention a major event requires the wind at 10 hPa and 60 N to turn easterly (below 0 m/s) [c2]. Such events occur about six times per decade in midwinter [c3]. A November event is rare; published counts differ [c4]. A weakening is not a major event.

sections.heading: What it may mean for weather
paragraphs: After weak-vortex events the surface often shows an Arctic Oscillation-like pattern over the following weeks, but not every time [c5]. The 2021 Texas freeze followed a January warming event; researchers disagree about whether one caused the other [c6].

sections.heading: What a popular video said
paragraphs: A video explainer from 26 October was careful that a freeze was not confirmed [c7], said the first week of November was not forecast to be freezing [c8], and said the European model flips the winds while the American model stops short [c9]. The table below rates each statement.

known: Observed (analysis, approximate chart reading): 10 hPa 60N zonal-mean wind about +23 m/s on 27 Oct, about +15 to +17 m/s on 29-30 Oct (source: CPC chart).
forecast: Model forecast (GFS/GEFS, issued 2026-10-30): ensemble members fall toward about 0 to +5 m/s around 10-13 Nov; a few slightly negative [f2].
Human forecast (CPC, issued 2026-10-29 3 pm EDT, confidence 'about average, 3 out of 5' for 6-10 days): above-normal temperatures favored for most of the contiguous US 4-12 Nov [f3].
unknown: Whether the wind reverses (no ECMWF forecast obtained; model counts quoted by news differ).
Whether any cold outbreak follows, and when: effects usually take weeks and vary from event to event.

definitions: A (weakening): 10 hPa 60N zonal-mean zonal wind at or below +5 m/s on at least one day from 1 to 15 Nov 2026.
B (major SSW, WMO type): the same wind below 0 m/s on at least one day from 1 to 30 Nov 2026.
C (sustained reversal): below 0 m/s for at least 5 consecutive days, the first before 15 Nov 2026.

D (surface response, evaluated only if B passes): daily or weekly mean Arctic Oscillation index negative on at least 7 of 14 days in a window starting 8 Nov to 8 Dec, and the NCEI CONUS monthly temperature anomaly for December 2026 below the 1991-2020 normal; each part reported separately.
